new.caption:
No RESP yet? It's not too late. Here's the catch-up plan.

SOUND FAMILIAR? "We'll start next year." Then the baby is five.

THE PART NOBODY TELLS YOU: your child's grant room builds up every year from birth, even if you never opened an RESP. The government matches 20% of what you save through the Canada Education Savings Grant.

YOU PUT IN, THEY ADD (per year):
• $1,000 in → $200 added
• $2,500 in → $500 added (the normal yearly max)
• $5,000 in → $1,000 added (*only if you have unused room from past years)

Catching up, the grant can be up to $1,000 a year, until the full $7,200 per child is used.

CAN'T DO $5,000? $2,500 a year still gets the full $500, and any amount gets 20% added.

THE DEADLINE: grants stop at the end of the year your child turns 17. At 16 and 17 they only qualify if at least $2,000 went in before the end of the year they turned 15, or $100 a year in any 4 earlier years. So for an older child, start now.

Do this: this week, ask your bank to open an RESP and use your catch-up room. Bring your child's SIN.

The rule that stays: the room waits for you, but not forever.

Send this to a parent who never opened one.

new.caption:
You can't spoil a newborn. Pick them up.

Why it works: the Canadian Paediatric Society says you can't “spoil” a baby by picking them up, and the American Academy of Pediatrics says that when you answer their calls for help, they cry less overall.

What helps, in order:
1. Check first: hungry, wet diaper, too hot or cold, fever.
2. Hold them close.
3. Dim the lights, shush, sway, or walk with them.

The catch: under 3 months with a fever? Get care right away.

Do this: next cry, pick them up first.

new.caption:
The crying has a peak. It often lands somewhere around 3 to 12 weeks, and it's usually over by 3 to 4 months.

Why that helps: a hard week isn't proof you're doing it wrong. It's a stage, and for most babies it eases.

What helps, in order (Canadian Paediatric Society):
1. Check first: hungry, wet diaper, too hot or cold, fever.
2. Hold them. You can't spoil a baby by picking them up.
3. Dim the lights, shush, sway, or walk them close to you.

The catch: under 3 months with a fever? Get care right away. And if it's too much, put baby in their crib, step out and take a moment. It's OK to ask for help.

Do this: next cry, check first, then hold close and sway.

new.caption:
Breastfed babies: 400 IU of vitamin D, every day.

Why: the Canadian Paediatric Society recommends a daily vitamin D supplement for breastfed babies, from birth until they get enough from their diet.

Formula-fed? Vitamin D is already added to infant formula, so most full-term babies on formula don't need drops.

The catch: babies in northern communities or with other risk factors may need more. Ask your baby's doctor or nurse.

Do this: ask your pharmacist which infant vitamin D drops to buy, and set a daily phone reminder.

Save this for your next pharmacy run.

new.caption:
It's OK to step away. Still crying, and you're at your limit? That happens to loving parents too.

Why it's OK: the Canadian Paediatric Society says that if you're feeling frustrated, take a deep breath, put your baby in a safe place like their crib, and take a moment to calm yourself. Taking a break can help, and it's OK to ask for help.

The plan:
1. Crib first: baby on their back.
2. Step out. Breathe. Take a moment.
3. Text your person: “Can you come?”
4. Go back when you're calmer.

Never shake a baby. Shaking can cause lifelong injury or even death.

If baby seems unwell, or is under 3 months with a fever, get care right away.

Do this: tonight, pick who you'll text, and tell them they're it.

Send this to every new parent. Part 2 of 2.

Follow for one calm thing a night, from bump to toddler.

General information only, not medical advice.
